CSCI-1969.description: This is an introductory programming course concentrating on key Artificial Intelligence (AI) concepts that underlie the development of AI tools. Topics will include classical and generative AI, searching and planning, and the real-world applications of these methods. The course will integrate extensive AI use in various programming tasks from assistive uses to cognitive offloading. Students will be asked to critically assess AI output from various angles, such as reliability, correctness, fairness, transparency, accountability, and privacy. Students will engage in real-world discussions of societal impacts of AI using case studies. Basic programming knowledge is required.
CSCI-1969.name: Ai Principles, Use & Impacts

CSCI-2961.description: A hands-on introduction to the foundations of data science and machine learning. Students will learn how different types of data—including tabular, sequential, image, and audio data—are represented and analyzed using mathematical and computational tools. Core topics include linear algebra, linear regression, logistic regression, optimization through gradient descent, neural networks, model evaluation, and overfitting. Through practical programming exercises, students will build and evaluate machine learning models, explore real-world datasets, and gain experience working with diverse data modalities. The course will also discuss elements of fairness, privacy, and responsible AI.
CSCI-2961.name: Principles Of Data & Ml

CSCI-4960.description: This course immerses students in collaborative development teams to design and build production-grade software using contemporary agile frameworks integrated with modern AI tools. Working in team environments, students will apply Scrum, Kanban, and Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) to navigate the full product lifecycle. Rather than using AI in isolation, teams will discover how AI can reshape group dynamics, i.e., accelerating backlog refinement, automating test scaffolding, and facilitating continuous integration while demanding rigorous human oversight during peer review. Students learn to wield AI as an amplifier for team velocity without compromising maintainability, security, or architectural integrity.
CSCI-4960.name: Agile Dev In The Age Of Ai

CSCI-4961.description: This course is designed to introduce students to the key aspects of CSCI inter-domain research, in particular in relation to AI. The course's primary goal is to make students aware of the technicalities related to formal research and to assist students in overcoming any common misconceptions that may exist. Further, this course focuses on both the use of AI in the research process and AI-specific domain areas. By completing this course, students will be able to conduct research in a more systematic and formal manner from the start.
CSCI-4961.name: Intro To Ai Research

CSCI-4962.description: This course will explore the challenges with ensuring the safety of modern autonomous systems. In the first half of the course, we will discuss some of the safety vulnerabilities of machine learning models, such as neural network robustness issues, and go over methods to alleviate these issues. In the second half, we will cover concepts from dynamical/autonomous system analysis and verification, once again with a focus on applying machine learning techniques and analyzing their safety. Students will get exposure to adversarial learning and reinforcement learning techniques, as well as to a number of neural network verification tools such as Reluplex, Verisig and others.
CSCI-4962.name: Safe Autonomy

CSCI-4963.description: A comprehensive introduction to the theory, architecture, training, evaluation, and applications of Large Language Models (LLMs). Students will study the mathematical and computational foundations underlying modern language models, including neural networks, attention mechanisms, transformers, self-supervised learning, scaling laws, alignment, and reasoning. The course examines how LLMs are trained, evaluated, fine-tuned, and deployed, while also addressing important challenges such as hallucinations, bias, privacy, robustness, and safety. Through programming assignments and hands-on projects, students will gain practical experience using and adapting state-of-the-art LLMs for real-world tasks. By the end of the course, students will understand both the capabilities and limitations of modern generative AI systems and be prepared for more advanced study in natural language processing and foundation models.
CSCI-4963.name: Foundations Of Llms

CSCI-4964.description: Deep Learning on Graphs is a course to explore state-of-the-art techniques in graph representation learning, with a particular emphasis on the emerging potential of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Graphs are widely used to represent data across various domains, including social science, linguistics, chemistry, biology, and physics, and GNNs have proven to be highly effective in facilitating computational tasks on these graphs. This course will cover topics such as network embedding, GNNs, properties of GNNs, and diverse applications of GNNs. In addition to lectures, students will be expected to read and discuss relevant literature, deliver presentations, and participate in research projects related to the subject matter.
CSCI-4964.name: Deep Learning On Graphs

CSCI-4965.description: In modern machine learning, we usually see more highlights of applications like GANs and deep neural networks. However, if we take a deeper look, the foundational connection between algorithm design and machine learning remains critical as ever. This course aims to explore the interplay between these two fields and demonstrate how they continue to drive innovation together. We will cover how algorithm design helps tackle major challenges in modern machine learning. You will learn the principles behind learning with efficiency to process very large datasets and techniques for learning from noisy, unreliable data. We will also explore how machine learning is facilitating algorithm design. We will examine how concepts originated from data science, e.g., differential privacy, are being integrated into general algorithms. We will also see how machine learning models can be used to dramatically boost the performance of algorithms. This is a rigorous, proof-based course focused on algorithm design. A solid foundation in algorithms, data structures, and mathematical maturity is required. Expect to spend most of your time with math and proofs in this course.
CSCI-4965.name: Algorithm Design & Modern Ml

CSCI-4967.description: This advanced theory course studies the design of "economic algorithms," such as student-school assignment, auctions, and multi-candidate elections, with an emphasis on improving their simplicity and quantifying their complexity. We will ask: How can we make the algorithms' outcomes transparent and their properties clear? What happens if participants are not perfectly rational, or the designer has only limited information or control? Topics may include market and information design, social choice theory, behavioral economics, interactive mechanisms, and communication complexity. For each topic covered, we will introduce classic results, study recent research papers, and have a problem set focused on theory. Prior experience with mathematical proofs (or significant effort) is required. Final course projects may be theory-focused (e.g., presenting or extending the results of a recent paper) or more-applied (e.g., running simulations, analyzing data, or building an implementation informed by course themes).
CSCI-4967.name: Designing Economic Algorithms

CSCI-4968.description: This is an advanced course in algorithms, looking specifically at algorithms for the related settings of facility location, clustering, and voting. Topics covered will include: approximation algorithms for facility location and k-median, metric distortion, computational social choice, voting, game theory and self-interested agents, fair clustering and fair committee selection, and forming algorithms which optimize multiple simultaneous objectives. Grades will be based mostly on homework assignments and on a research project which the students will complete in groups. No prior knowledge of game theory or social choice is required, although students should have had at least one previous course in algorithms.
CSCI-4968.name: Topics In Algorithms

CSCI-4969.description: In this course, we will look at the advanced methods employed in language models. Topics will cover energy-based models, diffusion language models, reasoning models, and agents. The course will focus on understanding how these methods work, reading the latest relevant papers, and also an emphasis on actual implementation.
CSCI-4969.name: Advanced Language Models

CSCI-4970.name: Deep Learning For Nat Lang Gen
